sections.heading: The idea

sections.figure_alt: A straight boundary with one side shaded.
sections.body_md:
A minimizer on a convex set need not have a zero gradient. The set can block the direction you would like to move. What replaces the zero-gradient test is a one-sided statement about feasible moves. From a candidate, every other feasible point has to look uphill, or at least not downhill, to first order.

Pair the gradient at the candidate with the vector from the candidate to any feasible point. The pairing has to be nonnegative. If some feasible point gives a negative pairing, a short step toward that point decreases the objective, so the candidate is not a local minimizer. Convexity of the set is what makes that step legal: the segment between the candidate and the feasible point stays inside the set.

An interior candidate has every direction and its opposite available, so the gradient itself is zero. When the objective is also convex, the inequality is enough for a global minimizer, because the graph stays above its tangent. Without that convexity the tangent test can hold at a maximum.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For differentiable \(f\) and convex \(\mathcal{X}\), a local minimizer \(x^\star\) satisfies
\[
\nabla f(x^\star)^T (x - x^\star) \ge 0 \qquad \text{for every } x \in \mathcal{X}.
\]
If \(f\) is convex, every feasible point that satisfies the inequality is a global minimizer. On a polygon it is enough to test the vertices, because a linear function attains its minimum there.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(f(t) = (t - 7)^2\) on the interval from \(0\) to \(1\), and test the right endpoint. The derivative is \(2(t - 7)\), so at \(1\) it equals \(-12\). The step from \(1\) back to \(0\) is \(-1\). The product is \((-12)(-1)\).

The anchor value is 12. Every feasible step from the right endpoint points left, and the derivative does too, so the product stays nonnegative. The unconstrained minimizer sits to the right of the interval.

The objective \(t^3\) on \([-2,\ 2]\) has a zero derivative at the origin, so the inequality holds, but the value at \(-2\) is \(-8\). The origin is not a minimizer.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A nonnegative pairing means feasible steps are not descent steps. Demanding a zero gradient on the boundary is a second slip: the gradient may point out of the set. Treating the inequality as a global certificate without convexity of the objective is a third. Necessity does not need that convexity. Sufficiency does. Checking one feasible point is not enough. On a polygon every vertex has to be tested.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The squared distance to a fixed point is a convex objective. Its variational inequality is the obtuse-angle test that characterizes the Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set. Projected gradient builds each step so that the inequality is the fixed-point condition. A conditional-gradient step uses the same inequality in linear form: the gradient's product with every feasible direction is tested by minimizing a linear function over the set.
